title: ABCD SYNDROME
alt_titles: ALBINISM, BLACK LOCK, CELL MIGRATION DISORDER OF THE NEUROCYTES OF THE GUT, AND DEAFNESS

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that ABCD syndrome (ABCDS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the endothelin receptor type B gene (EDNRB; 131244) on chromosome 13q22.3.

checks.claim: ABCD syndrome (ABCDS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the endothelin receptor type B gene (EDNRB).
checks.evidence_quote: ABCD syndrome is caused by a homozygous mutation in the EDNRB gene.
checks.explanation: Title states it.

checks.claim: The EDNRB gene is located on chromosome 13q22.3.
checks.evidence_quote: ABCD syndrome is caused by a homozygous mutation in the EDNRB gene.
checks.explanation: Chromosomal location is standard nomenclature added by the draft; gene is the one named in the paper.

paragraphs.text: ABCD syndrome is an autosomal recessive neural crest disorder (neurocristopathy) (Gross et al., 1995; Verheij et al., 2002). The name, given by Gross et al. (1995), is an acronym for albinism, black lock, cell migration disorder of the neurocytes of the gut, and deafness. Verheij et al. (2002) suggested that ABCD syndrome is not a separate entity but an expression of Shah-Waardenburg syndrome (Waardenburg syndrome type 4), which is caused by EDNRB mutations.

checks.claim: ABCD syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: ABCD syndrome is an autosomal recessive syndrome characterized by albinism, black lock, cell migration disorder of the neurocytes of the gut (Hirschsprung disease [HSCR]), and deafness.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: ABCD syndrome is a neural crest disorder (neurocristopathy).
checks.evidence_quote: It represents a new neural crest syndrome with autosomal-recessive inheritance.
checks.explanation: The abstract calls it a neural crest syndrome, which is what neurocristopathy means.

checks.claim: Gross et al. (1995) gave ABCD syndrome its name.
checks.evidence_quote: Autosomal-recessive neural crest syndrome with albinism, black lock, cell migration disorder of the neurocytes of the gut, and deafness: ABCD syndrome.
checks.explanation: The paper's title gives the condition the name ABCD syndrome.

checks.claim: The name ABCD syndrome is an acronym for albinism, black lock, cell migration disorder of the neurocytes of the gut, and deafness.
checks.evidence_quote: albinism, black lock, cell migration disorder of the neurocytes of the gut, and deafness: ABCD syndrome.
checks.explanation: The title spells out the acronym exactly as the draft does.

checks.claim: Verheij et al. (2002) suggested that ABCD syndrome is not a separate entity but an expression of Shah-Waardenburg syndrome (Waardenburg syndrome type 4).
checks.evidence_quote: We therefore suggest that ABCD syndrome is not a separate entity, but an expression of Shah-Waardenburg syndrome.
checks.explanation: Stated directly; WS4 is a synonym.

checks.claim: Shah-Waardenburg syndrome (Waardenburg syndrome type 4) is caused by EDNRB mutations.
checks.evidence_quote: the endothelin B receptor (EDNRB) gene, a gene known to be involved in Shah-Waardenburg syndrome
checks.explanation: Abstract states EDNRB is involved in Shah-Waardenburg syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Gross et al. (1995) described a child of Kurdish origin who had albinism, a black lock of hair, intestinal aganglionosis (Hirschsprung disease), and deafness. Gross et al. (1995) regarded this combination of features as a new neural crest syndrome and named it with the acronym ABCD.

checks.claim: Gross et al. (1995) described a child with ABCD syndrome who was of Kurdish origin.
checks.evidence_quote: She was the 14th child of consanguineous Kurdish parents.
checks.explanation: The patient's parents were Kurdish.

checks.claim: The child with ABCD syndrome described by Gross et al. (1995) had albinism.
checks.evidence_quote: We report on a macrosomic newborn girl with albinism
checks.explanation: The abstract states the patient had albinism.

checks.claim: The child with ABCD syndrome described by Gross et al. (1995) had a black lock of hair.
checks.evidence_quote: a black lock at the right temporo-occipital region
checks.explanation: The abstract states the patient had a black lock.

checks.claim: The child with ABCD syndrome described by Gross et al. (1995) had intestinal aganglionosis (Hirschsprung disease).
checks.evidence_quote: Biopsy showed aganglionosis of the large intestine, and total absence of neurocytes and nerve fibers in the small intestine
checks.explanation: Aganglionosis of the large intestine is stated. The paper does not use the term 'Hirschsprung disease', and the defect also reached the small intestine.

checks.claim: The child with ABCD syndrome described by Gross et al. (1995) had deafness.
checks.evidence_quote: Bilateral deafness was confirmed by brainstem auditory-evoked potentials.
checks.explanation: The abstract states the patient had deafness.

checks.claim: Gross et al. (1995) regarded the combination of albinism, black lock, intestinal aganglionosis, and deafness as a new neural crest syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: A syndrome of albinism, black lock, deafness, and a total lack of intestinal neural innervation has not yet been reported. It represents a new neural crest syndrome
checks.explanation: The authors present this combination of features as a new neural crest syndrome.

checks.claim: Gross et al. (1995) named the new neural crest syndrome with the acronym ABCD.
checks.evidence_quote: cell migration disorder of the neurocytes of the gut, and deafness: ABCD syndrome.
checks.explanation: The title names the syndrome ABCD.

paragraphs.text: The family reported by Gross et al. (1995) suggested autosomal recessive inheritance. Verheij et al. (2002), who described ABCD syndrome as autosomal recessive, found a homozygous EDNRB mutation in the index patient of an ABCD syndrome family.

checks.claim: The family with ABCD syndrome reported by Gross et al. (1995) suggested autosomal recessive inheritance.
checks.evidence_quote: She was the 14th child of consanguineous Kurdish parents. Four sibs of our patient had the same syndrome and died a few days after birth. The other 9 sibs are well
checks.explanation: The parents were consanguineous and several sibs were affected, and the authors conclude that inheritance is autosomal recessive.

checks.claim: Verheij et al. (2002) described ABCD syndrome as autosomal recessive.
checks.evidence_quote: ABCD syndrome is an autosomal recessive syndrome
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Verheij et al. (2002) found a homozygous EDNRB mutation in the index patient of a family with ABCD syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: we screened DNA of the index patient of the ABCD syndrome family for mutations in the endothelin B receptor (EDNRB) gene, a gene known to be involved in Shah-Waardenburg syndrome. A homozygous nonsense mutation in exon 3 (R201X) of the EDNRB gene was found.
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

paragraphs.text: In the index patient of a family with ABCD syndrome, Verheij et al. (2002) identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the EDNRB gene (arg201-to-ter; R201X). They concluded that ABCD syndrome is not a separate entity but an expression of Shah-Waardenburg syndrome (Waardenburg syndrome type 4), which is caused by EDNRB mutation.

checks.claim: Verheij et al. (2002) identified a nonsense mutation in the EDNRB gene, arg201-to-ter (R201X), in the index patient of a family with ABCD syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: A homozygous nonsense mutation in exon 3 (R201X) of the EDNRB gene was found.
checks.explanation: Found in the index patient of the ABCD family.

checks.claim: The EDNRB R201X mutation was homozygous in the index patient of the ABCD syndrome family studied by Verheij et al. (2002).
checks.evidence_quote: A homozygous nonsense mutation in exon 3 (R201X) of the EDNRB gene was found.
checks.explanation: Homozygous stated.

checks.claim: Verheij et al. (2002) concluded that ABCD syndrome is not a separate entity but an expression of Shah-Waardenburg syndrome (Waardenburg syndrome type 4).
checks.evidence_quote: We therefore suggest that ABCD syndrome is not a separate entity, but an expression of Shah-Waardenburg syndrome.
checks.explanation: Paper 'suggests' rather than firmly concludes.

checks.claim: Shah-Waardenburg syndrome (Waardenburg syndrome type 4) is caused by EDNRB mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: the endothelin B receptor (EDNRB) gene, a gene known to be involved in Shah-Waardenburg syndrome
checks.explanation: Abstract states EDNRB is involved in Shah-Waardenburg syndrome.

paragraphs.text: In the index patient of a family with ABCD syndrome, Verheij et al. (2002) identified a homozygous arg201-to-ter (R201X) nonsense mutation in the EDNRB gene.

checks.claim: Verheij et al. (2002) identified an arg201-to-ter (R201X) nonsense mutation in the EDNRB gene in the index patient of a family with ABCD syndrome.
checks.evidence_quote: A homozygous nonsense mutation in exon 3 (R201X) of the EDNRB gene was found.
checks.explanation: Stated directly for the index patient.

checks.claim: The EDNRB R201X mutation was homozygous in the index patient of the ABCD syndrome family studied by Verheij et al. (2002).
checks.evidence_quote: A homozygous nonsense mutation in exon 3 (R201X) of the EDNRB gene was found.
checks.explanation: Homozygous stated.
